abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic framework for analyzing the dynamics of evolutionary algorithms that fundamentally reconceptualizes how population-based search mechanisms operate. While traditional schema theory and Markov chain analyses have provided valuable insights, they fail to capture the essential relationship between information flow and adaptive behavior in evolving populations. We propose modeling the evolutionary search process as an information-theoretic channel where selection acts as a lossy compression operator and variation as an information injection mechanism. This perspective enables rigorous derivation of fundamental limits on evolutionary search performance using tools from rate-distortion theory and the information bottleneck method. We establish that the expected fitness improvement per generation is bounded by the mutual information rate between parent and offspring populations, normalized by the population's internal entropy. The framework provides exact conditions for when evolutionary computation can outperform random search, characterizing the critical relationship between population diversity and selection pressure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework naturally explains the empirical success of fitness inheritance mechanisms and reveals why certain problem structures are inherently more amenable to evolutionary approaches. This theoretical foundation offers new design principles for evolutionary algorithms and establishes connections to statistical physics approaches while providing predictive power for algorithm behavior on unseen problem instances.

This paper advances the runtime analysis of evolutionary algorithms for dynamic optimization problems by introducing a refined drift condition that accounts for population diversity as a dynamic resource. Existing theoretical analyses of evolutionary algorithms in changing environments rely on bounding the expected time to re-converge after a change, but they neglect the crucial interplay between retained diversity and adaptation speed. We develop a novel multi-type branching process model that tracks the abundance of different genotypes throughout the optimization process and characterize how environmental changes affect this distribution. Our main result establishes that the expected re-convergence time depends on the spectral properties of the mutation operator and the magnitude of fitness changes, providing a precise characterization of when memory mechanisms in evolutionary algorithms are beneficial. We prove that for moderate change frequencies, maintaining a diverse population reduces re-convergence time by a factor proportional to the logarithm of the population size, while for rapid changes, a genetically diverse population becomes essential for maintaining reasonable performance. The analysis yields specific recommendations for adapting mutation rates and population sizing in response to detected environmental changes. Experimental validation on benchmark dynamic optimization problems confirms the theoretical predictions and demonstrates that algorithms incorporating the derived guidelines outperform existing approaches.

We introduce EvoCo-DL, a novel evolutionary computation architecture that fundamentally integrates evolutionary search with deep representation learning to create a self-improving optimization system. Unlike conventional evolutionary algorithms that treat fitness evaluation as a black-box function and prior knowledge as external input, EvoCo-DL evolves both the candidate solutions and the representation space in which those solutions are evaluated through a coevolutionary process. The system consists of two coevolving populations: a solution population that undergoes variation and selection, and a representation population that evolves neural network architectures to construct increasingly informative feature spaces. These populations influence each other through a bidirectional feedback mechanism where successful solutions provide training signals for representation improvement, while improved representations enable more effective solution evaluation. This mutualistic relationship creates an autocatalytic improvement loop that accelerates optimization convergence. EvoCo-DL employs a multi-objective selection scheme that balances solution quality with representation interpretability and computational efficiency. We evaluate the system on complex real-world optimization tasks including neural architecture search, automated machine learning, and robotic controller design. Results demonstrate that EvoCo-DL discovers high-quality solutions while simultaneously learning representations that transfer across problem instances, representing a fundamental advance in how evolutionary computation can leverage learned knowledge.

This paper presents MultiScale-EMA, a significantly enhanced multi-objective evolutionary algorithm that addresses the critical challenge of solution diversity maintenance in high-dimensional objective spaces. Existing algorithms struggle to balance convergence and diversity when scaling to many-objective problems, often sacrificing one for the other. MultiScale-EMA introduces a hierarchical clustering mechanism that decomposes the objective space at multiple scales, enabling adaptive management of solution diversity based on problem characteristics. The algorithm employs a dynamic reference point generation strategy that adapts to the geometry of the Pareto front, placing reference directions more densely in regions of high curvature or where solutions are sparse. We incorporate an improved crowding distance calculation that accounts for both objective space proximity and decision space diversity, preventing premature convergence to limited regions of the Pareto front. The system includes an adaptive mating restriction mechanism that promotes exploration of underrepresented regions while maintaining selective pressure toward the true Pareto front. Extensive experimentation on standard many-objective benchmark problems with 5 to 30 objectives demonstrates that MultiScale-EMA achieves superior performance in both convergence metrics and diversity preservation compared to state-of-the-art algorithms including NSGA-III and MOEA/D. The algorithm exhibits particularly strong performance on problems with complex Pareto front geometries and uneven solution distributions.
